variants.name: std::async futures fanned out over a bounded partition (C++11)
variants.implementation_notes: C++11's <future> gives the master two library pieces: std::async launches each sub-task and std::future::get() joins it, rethrowing whatever the sub-task threw. Because the default policy is async|deferred - the implementation may run the callable lazily in the calling thread - pass std::launch::async explicitly or you may never get parallelism. Fan out at most roughly std::thread::hardware_concurrency() tasks (one future per core-sized partition) since oversubscription costs context switches, and remember that future::wait/get on the last future is the join point while the shared state is the aggregation slot. For a long-lived worker set with a queue, a pool (oneTBB, OpenMP taskloop) is the better fit; std::async per task is convenient but not a pool.
pitfalls: The default launch policy may defer execution into the calling thread; without std::launch::async the 'workers' may never run in parallel.
std::async's returned future blocks in its destructor when it came from a truly async call, so a discarded future can serialise the master at an unexpected point.
Exceptions are captured per future and rethrown at get(); the first get() that throws leaves the remaining sub-tasks running, so decide whether to discard or join them.
Shared state captured by reference must be immutable during the parallel phase - the compiler will not catch a data race, and none of the futures orders the writes.

variants.name: std::jthread worker pool with cooperative stop_token cancellation (C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: std::jthread is the C++20 worker type: its destructor requests a stop and joins, so a pool of jthreads needs no explicit shutdown bookkeeping, and each worker receives a std::stop_token it polls (stop_requested() or stop_callback) inside the work loop. The master keeps the partition/dispatch/combine responsibilities and calls request_stop() to end a batch early; the join is still the destructor. Use this variant when the toolchain is C++20 and sub-tasks are long-running enough that cooperative cancellation matters; the stop_token replaces ad-hoc atomic stop flags and makes the master's cancellation lever explicit.
pitfalls: A worker that ignores its stop_token keeps running: cancellation is cooperative, so blocking calls must be interruptible (or polled) for request_stop() to take effect.
The condition variable must wait on (queue not empty || stop requested); otherwise a stop request never wakes a sleeping worker and the destructor's join hangs.
Results written by workers must be combined after the join - jthread's destructor order is the only synchronisation guarantee, not the stop signal.

variants.name: OpenMP taskloop over a parallel region (toolchain-provided tasks)
variants.idiom_name: #pragma omp taskloop (or parallel for) with reduction
variants.implementation_notes: OpenMP moves the decomposition into the toolchain: a parallel region starts the team, taskloop partitions the associated loop into explicit tasks (creating an implicit taskgroup that joins them) and a reduction clause replaces the hand-written combine. The master is the encountering thread of the parallel region; the workers are the team. Prefer this variant when the work is a regular loop over independent iterations and you want the compiler to handle scheduling, or when a parallel for with reduction is enough - the explicit master/worker roles then exist only implicitly, which is the trade: less code, less control over dispatch and failure handling.
pitfalls: taskloop without single executes once per team thread, duplicating every task; wrap it in single (or use parallel for).
The reduction variable's combine is associative-by-contract but floating-point summation order is unspecified, so results differ run to run unless the reduction is structured.
A stray data-sharing attribute (shared instead of firstprivate/default(none)) turns independent sub-tasks into a race.
